newsitem.title: USA: Conditions said tough for U.S. woman in Peru jail.
newsitem.headline: Conditions said tough for U.S. woman in Peru jail.

text.p: The United States said on Monday an American woman serving a life sentence in prison for terrorism in Peru was being held under "very very tough conditions" and Washington was monitoring her treatment.

"She is being held in very, very tough conditions in a prison, I understand well above 10,000 feet (3,000 metres) in the mountains of Peru ... one could describe them only charitably as minimal. They are very difficult," State Department deputy spokesman Glyn Davies said of Lori Berenson, 27.

Last January a Peruvian military court convicted Berenson of treason and sentenced her to life in prison for association with Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement, a pro-Cuban group known for violent attacks and kidnappings.
Her lawyers argued she knew of no terrorist plans that the group might have had and Berenson contended she was persecuted for fighting against poverty and injustice.
Diplomats assigned to the U.S. embassay in Lima, Peru, visit Berenson monthly and bring her mail, food and other packages from family and friends, Davies said.

Davies spoke after the woman's parents, Mark and Rhoda Berenson of New York City, visited their daughter for the first time on Saturday in Peru and told reporters she was living in inhumane conditions and suffering several ailments because of poor nutrition, high altitude and extreme cold.
Davies said the International Committee of the Red Cross looked into Berenson's case and found her prison conditions "generally considered to meet bare minimum acceptable conditions or standards."
He noted "there are a number of Americans overseas in tough prisons."
In Berenson's case, he said the U.S. role has been to ensure the woman is not discriminated against because she is an American.
Also, U.S. officials continued to press the Peruvian government for her appeal to be handled by a civilian court because her original trial was in a secretive military court.
"We did not recognise that the decision made by the military court or the process was one that met minimally acceptable standards of international due process," he said.

Davies said the United States has a treaty with Peru that would allow Berenson to serve her sentence in the United States. But Berenson did not invoke that process, apparently because she would have to first confess guilt.
